name: Helen Keller Intl: vitamin A supplementation and NTD treatment (charityevals)
summary: Helen Keller Intl supports ministries of health in 14 African countries to give vitamin A twice a year to 47 million children under five, and to treat 32 million people a year for neglected tropical diseases (river blindness, filariasis, trachoma, worms) in seven African countries. For its fiscal year to June 2025, the two programmes together come to the bottom line shown, in years of healthy life per $1,000: vitamin A by averting under-five deaths (a 12% cut in mortality from the Cochrane review), NTD treatment by the later-life income gain of dewormed children (adults' illness from river blindness, filariasis and trachoma isn't valued). The biggest uncertainties are how much of the old trials' effect carries to today's campaigns, how many children routine care would have reached without the campaigns, and the worm burden behind the deworming income gain. The rest of the nutrition programme (malnutrition treatment, gardens, maternal supplements and more, about 45% of cash programme spending) has outcome counts for some activities but no spending split, so it isn't modelled: the result covers vitamin A and NTDs, about half of cash programme spending.

source.title: Helen Keller Intl, Form 990 for the year ended June 2025, Schedule O, Part III line 4b
source.quote: TO REACH OVER 47 MILLION CHILDREN UNDER THE AGE OF FIVE WITH TWO DOSES OF VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION

rows.explainer: Helen Keller's own count (administrative, with ministries of health) for the fiscal year: 47 million children, two doses each; its website gives 94.4 million capsules for 2025, which matches two per child. By country (2025 one-page fact sheets): DRC 10.8m, Niger 7.3m, Cameroon 6m, Côte d'Ivoire 4.7m, Guinea 3.7m, Mali 3.6m, Burkina Faso 1.6m, Mozambique 1.4m, Madagascar 1m (the annual report's 2.9 million Malagasy children is the total since the programme began), Kenya 0.95m, Senegal 0.57m, Tanzania 0.49m, the remaining 4.9m (Nigeria and Sierra Leone, no sheet found). The annual report's 'nearly 7 million Malian children' is about twice Mali's sheet (3.6m) and Mali's under-five population, so it reads as doses; the sheet is used. Not an independent coverage survey: the shortfall is in vas_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Annual all-cause mortality of children 6–59 months where Helen Keller gives vitamin A

source.title: UN IGME estimates 2023 via World Bank WDI (SH.DYN.MORT, SP.DYN.IMRT.IN, SH.DYN.NMRT)

rows.explainer: UN IGME 2023 (via the World Bank API) under-five, infant and neonatal mortality, per country, weighted by the children reached in each (see vas_people_reached). Deaths from 6 to 59 months per birth = U5MR − NMR − half the post-neonatal infant deaths (assumed at 1–5 months), divided by the survivors at six months and by 4.5 years: 0.0105 a child-year (reach-weighted U5MR 87 per 1,000; Niger and Nigeria 0.0146–0.0148, Kenya, Tanzania and Senegal under 0.003). Range: a quarter to three quarters of post-neonatal infant deaths before six months (0.0094–0.0117), widened for national rather than district rates.

rows.label: Reduction in all-cause mortality from vitamin A supplementation, 6–59 months

source.title: Imdad A et al., Vitamin A supplementation for preventing morbidity and mortality in children from six months to five years of age, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022 (abstract, PubMed)
source.quote: risk ratio (RR) 0.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.83 to 0.93; high-certainty evidence

rows.explainer: Cochrane review (Imdad et al. 2022): risk ratio 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93) for all-cause mortality, 19 trials, 1.2 million children, high-certainty evidence; the 95% CI as the range. All-cause, so indirect deaths are included.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Vitamin A is given to children aged 6 to 59 months only, so every death averted is under five.

rows.explainer: The site's one figure for the short-term benefits of less illness from vitamin A (@givewell_common.short_term_consequences_of_reduced_infectious_disease_m).

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per child reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: vitamin A is given to children 6–59 months, not to pregnant women; NTD drugs aren't given in pregnancy.

rows.label: Vitamin A: later-life income of the children saved, as a share of the deaths' value (the site's shared shortcut)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for programmes that save young children's lives without modelling their later income (@givewell_shared.income_to_mortality_value_ratio), the same shortcut the New Incentives model reads.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gained by doubling consumption
rows.explainer: ln 2, by definition: the ratio above is at GiveWell's valuation of one unit of value per doubling of consumption (1/ln 2 per unit of ln consumption), which the rescaling below replaces with the income slider.

rows.label: Vitamin A: that ratio at your discount rate and values
rows.explainer: Rescaled as in the New Incentives model: the present value of 40 years of income at your discount rate, starting after the site's wait for a micronutrient programme (@givewell_shared.years_until_income_benefits_iron), over the same at the ratio's own rate and wait (malaria's), times the income slider over 1/ln 2, divided by the weight on a life (which the deaths' value it multiplies already carries).

rows.label: Share of people treated for NTDs who are school-age children dewormed (albendazole or praziquantel)
rows.explainer: Judgment: the long-run income gain is measured for children dewormed at school age. Helen Keller treats whole communities for river blindness and lymphatic filariasis (ivermectin with albendazole, which also clears intestinal worms) and school-age children for schistosomiasis and worms. Anchor: Mali's sheet counts 4 million children 5–14 treated among Mali's 7.5 million people reached; Sierra Leone treats 1.5 million children a year for schistosomiasis; children 5–14 are about 30% of these populations. Adults' gains from less filariasis and river blindness are in ntd_morbidity_value_ratio.

rows.label: Consumption gain in adulthood from two to three more years of childhood deworming (Kenya trial)

source.title: Hamory J, Miguel E, Walker M, Kremer M, Baird S. Twenty-year economic impacts of deworming. PNAS 2021 (abstract via Europe PMC; pnas.org refused and PMC showed a bot check)
source.quote: Individuals who received two to three additional years of childhood deworming experienced a 14% gain in consumption expenditures and 13% increase in hourly earnings.

rows.explainer: Hamory et al. 2021, twenty-year follow-up of the Busia school deworming trial: +14% consumption expenditure (+13% hourly earnings). Range from no effect to twice the estimate, the trial's imprecision.

rows.label: Additional years of deworming behind that gain

source.title: Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS (abstract via Europe PMC)
source.quote: Individuals who received two to three additional years of childhood deworming experienced a 14% gain in consumption expenditures

rows.explainer: 'Two to three additional years' (Hamory et al. 2021).

rows.label: Kenya trial schools: pupils with at least one moderate-to-heavy worm infection at baseline

source.title: Miguel E, Kremer M. Worms: identifying impacts on education and health in the presence of treatment externalities. Econometrica 72(1), 2004
source.quote: Ninety-two percent of surveyed pupils had at least one helminth infection and thirty-seven percent had at least one moderate-to-heavy helminth infection

rows.explainer: Miguel and Kremer (2004), the trial behind the income gain, Busia 1998.

rows.label: Helen Keller's NTD districts: school-age children with a moderate-to-heavy worm or schistosome infection
rows.explainer: Judgment from surveys in Helen Keller's countries after a decade or more of mass treatment: Burkina Faso, 16 districts 2023–24, schistosomiasis prevalence 2.4% with heavy-intensity schistosomiasis 0.9% (Zongo et al. 2025, PMID 39913556; 1–4 years after the last rounds); Sierra Leone 2016, any intestinal worm 18.3% but only 0.33% of children with moderate or heavy hookworm (PMID 31262367; about 8 months after the last round). Both are under 1% moderate-to-heavy for the worms they measure; the best guess adds schistosomiasis hotspots (29 Burkina health areas above 1% heavy; Mali, Niger) and reinfection between rounds, since these post-treatment levels stand in for the burden a year's treatment removes. 2% (0.5–6%). Busia's 37% used moderate-infection thresholds lower than WHO's for hookworm and whipworm, so a like-for-like ratio would be somewhat higher: the high end allows for it.

rows.label: Worm burden where Helen Keller treats, against the Kenya trial's
rows.explainer: Moderate-to-heavy infection here ÷ in the trial's schools: the income gain is scaled by the burden (about 0.05).

rows.label: Dose of Helen Keller's annual treatment against the trial's
rows.explainer: Judgment: the trial gave albendazole every six months (and praziquantel yearly where schistosomiasis was common); Helen Keller's mass drug administration is mostly once a year. Worms reinfect within months, so one round clears less of the year's burden than two, but not half as much: 0.7 (0.5–1).

rows.label: NTD branch: later-life income gain per person treated, ln(consumption) per year
rows.formula: ntd_child_share * ln(1 + deworming_consumption_gain) / deworming_extra_years * ntd_worm_burden_ratio * ntd_rounds_vs_trial
rows.explainer: Per person treated for one year: the children's share × the trial's ln gain per extra year of deworming × the worm burden here × the dose against the trial's.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for deworming (@givewell_shared.years_until_income_benefits_deworming).

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person treated, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times (INV-13).

rows.label: NTD branch: dewormed children's short-term illness averted, as a share of the branch's income value
rows.explainer: Judgment: the short-term illness of the same children whose later income is counted (anaemia, abdominal pain, schistosomiasis's blood loss), so it moves with the same worm burden. 0.06 (0.02–0.15), anchored on vitamin A's short-term illness share (@givewell_common.short_term_consequences_of_reduced_infectious_disease_m, 6%); long-run non-income gains are separate (ntd_non_income_share). Adults' illness from river blindness, filariasis and trachoma (blindness, lymphoedema, trichiasis) isn't valued: the site has no shared value for disability in units of value, so the NTD branch understates (What isn't modelled). Rough size: mass ivermectin under APOC averted an estimated 8.2 million DALYs in 1995–2010 (Coffeng et al. 2013, PMID 23383355), on the order of 0.01 a treatment or less; at the site's defaults this judgment puts the missing value at a few per cent of the result.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the mortality and income benefits
rows.explainer: For reading only: the two branches' own ratios (vitamin A on its deaths and income, NTD on its income), weighted by value.

rows.label: Internal validity of the vitamin A trials, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for vitamin A and iron trials (@givewell_common.internal_validity_adjustment_vas_iron).

rows.label: External validity: the trials' setting against today's campaigns, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Judgment: most trials in the Cochrane pool ran in the 1980s and 1990s, when vitamin A deficiency was more severe and measles and diarrhoea, the causes vitamin A acts on, were a larger share of child deaths; measles vaccination and oral rehydration have since cut those deaths, so the same relative cut in all-cause mortality is likely smaller today. The pooled effect already includes the largest recent trial (DEVTA), so no separate discount for it. Against that, Helen Keller's countries still report deficiency in more than half of children (DRC 61%, Côte d'Ivoire 60%, Burkina Faso over 50%, Mozambique 69%; Madagascar 1 in 8), and the baseline mortality used is today's. 0.75 (0.5–1). Anchor: the shared internal-validity figure (0.8) covers only the trials' own bias.

rows.label: Vitamin A: evidence adjustment (internal × external validity)
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Vitamin A: share of doses children wouldn't have got through routine care
rows.explainer: Judgment, one question only: of the doses given in the campaigns Helen Keller supports, the share a child would not have received through routine care alone (1 − routine coverage ÷ campaign coverage). Whether another funder would have paid for the campaigns is leverage_funging's question. Anchors: Tanzania, 13% coverage under routine immunisation-visit delivery against 76% under twice-yearly campaigns (Masanja et al. 2006, PMID 17078872), about 0.83; 44 coverage surveys in 13 African countries (Janmohamed et al. 2017, PMID 28532531), door-to-door 91% against fixed-site plus outreach 63%, about 0.3 against that stronger fixed-site alternative; Senegal after its move to routine delivery about 0.5. 0.65 (0.4–0.85).
